# Build essentials {#sec-build}

This chapter is not a CMake course. It covers the four ideas you need to read and extend a
modern Qt build; the CMake and Qt documentation covers the rest.

## Targets and usage requirements {#sec-targets}

A **target** is something CMake builds: a library or an executable. It carries its sources,
its include paths and its dependencies. When one target links another, it inherits the
other's **usage requirements**, and the keyword decides how far they travel.

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
add_library(shapes STATIC src/Recognizer.cpp)
target_include_directories(shapes PUBLIC include)

add_library(storage STATIC Storage.cpp)
target_link_libraries(storage
    PUBLIC shapes         # <1>
    PRIVATE glaze::glaze  # <2>
)

add_executable(app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE storage)  # <3>
```
1. `storage`'s own headers use `shapes` types, so its users need `shapes` too.
2. JSON handling is an implementation detail; `storage`'s users never see glaze.
3. `app` gets `storage` and, through it, `shapes`, but not glaze's headers.

The rule of thumb: **PUBLIC** if the dependency appears in your headers, **PRIVATE** if it
appears only in your `.cpp` files. Set everything on targets, never through global
variables, and the build describes your architecture.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [cmake-buildsystem(7)](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-buildsystem.7.html)
:::

## Qt's CMake API {#sec-qt-cmake}

Qt adds a handful of commands on top of CMake. Three of them cover a Qt Quick application:

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.31)
project(Sketchbook VERSION 0.1.0 LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(Qt6 6.12 REQUIRED COMPONENTS Quick)
qt_standard_project_setup(REQUIRES 6.12)  # <1>

qt_add_executable(app main.cpp)
qt_add_qml_module(app                     # <2>
    URI App
    QML_FILES Main.qml
    SOURCES AppController.cpp AppController.hpp
)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE Qt::Quick)
```
1. Turns on Qt's code generators (such as moc) and the defaults of the Qt version you name.
2. A **QML module**: a name to import (`URI`), its QML files and C++ sources, built and
   checked together.

You will meet `qt_add_qml_module()` again in @sec-cpp-qml. It is the one command that ties
C++ and QML together.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `CMakeLists.txt`, `src/app/CMakeLists.txt` ·
**Read more:** [Getting started with CMake (Qt)](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/cmake-get-started.html)
:::

## Static and dynamic libraries {#sec-linking}

A library reaches your program in one of two ways.

A **static** library (`.a`, `.lib`) is copied into your executable when it is linked. The
result is one file with everything inside.

A **dynamic** library (`.so`, `.dylib`, `.dll`) stays a separate file. The operating system
loads it when the program starts, so it must be on the user's machine.

| | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Joins the program | at link time | at start-up |
| On the user's machine | nothing extra | the library, from the system or shipped with the app |
| Memory | one copy per program | one copy shared by every program that uses it |
| Updates | rebuild the program | replace the library |

The last two rows explain why systems share libraries such as the C runtime or OpenSSL:
memory is used once, and a security fix reaches every program at once. For your app, the
choice decides what you must ship (@sec-shipping) and, for LGPL libraries such as Qt, what
the license requires (@sec-licenses).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Works on my machine
A dynamic library that exists on your computer but not on the user's makes the program fail
at start-up. Every dynamic dependency is something you must ship or require.
:::

## Presets: the build is one command {#sec-presets}

`CMakePresets.json` records how to configure, build, test and package the project. Everyone,
your CI included, runs the same command; nobody has to remember flags.

```{.json filename="CMakePresets.json"}
{
  "version": 6,
  "configurePresets": [
    {
      "name": "dev",
      "generator": "Ninja",
      "binaryDir": "${sourceDir}/build/${presetName}",
      "cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE": "Debug" }
    }
  ],
  "buildPresets": [{ "name": "dev", "configurePreset": "dev" }],
  "testPresets": [{ "name": "dev", "configurePreset": "dev" }],
  "workflowPresets": [
    {
      "name": "dev",
      "steps": [
        { "type": "configure", "name": "dev" },
        { "type": "build", "name": "dev" },
        { "type": "test", "name": "dev" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

```sh
cmake --workflow --preset dev
```

Settings that belong to one machine, such as the path to your Qt or a build folder outside a
synced directory, go into `CMakeUserPresets.json`. It can inherit from the shared presets and
stays out of version control.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `CMakePresets.json`, with `dev`, `asan`, `release` and `vcpkg-qt` workflows ·
**Read more:** [cmake-presets(7)](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/cmake-presets.7.html)
:::
